newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica Reserve Bank doesn't want shortage too low.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica Reserve Bank doesn't want shortage too low.

text.p: The Reserve Bank was reluctant for the money market shortage to fall too far and could drain liquidity if it declined further, a central bank official said on Thursday.

Roelf du Plooy, assistant general manager at the central bank's money and capital markets division, said that while the bank did not target any specific level on the shortage, it could act if the shortage fell further.
"At this stage it could give the wrong signals to the market that the Bank is softening on its monetary policy," he said.
"If it looks like the shortage is going to drop substantially then we will have to do something...maybe through swaps or selling other paper into the market.
"Personally I think we would like to see it increase gradually above six billion rand," he added.
On Wednesday the shortage fell to 5.821 billion rand from 6.178 billion previously.
Du Plooy said the fall in the shortage overnight had resulted from a mismatch in government flows.

"The main reason is that government expenditure for yesterday was much higher than we anticipated so instead of being able to neutralise the effect of that by withdrawing money from the Tax and Loan accounts, we withdrew less money than was necessary," he said.
In recent weeks, he said the shortage had fallen from around the eight to nine billion rand level as a result of foreign inflows.
"We have seen a lot of foreign inflows into the country and that has definitely added some liquidity to the money market."
The unwinding of swaps used to mop up excess liquidity created by the inflow of about $1 billion from the partial privatisation of telecommunications utility Telkom had also boosted liquidity.

"With the Telkom money that came in we did a total of about three billion rand in foreign exchange swaps. They unwound after about 10 days or so and the effect of that also put some liquidity back into the system," he said.
He said that the total three billion has now been unwound.
"Whether we drain it again depends on what happens to the shortage."

Du Plooy said that the central bank had tried to manage the swaps in such a way that their expansionary effect would be neutralised by the contractionary effect of a rise in notes and coins in circulation at month-end.
Because notes and coins had been volatile at the end of May, this had resulted in volatility in the shortage, he said.
Du Plooy added that because the shortage had fallen on Wednesday as a result of the mismatch, the shortage could be expected to rise again on Thursday.
